Galaxy Genome Wiki:
[[File:Galaxy Genome.png|thumb]]
'''Galaxy Genome''' is a space simulator for iOS and Android by SKV Games.
You start in an [[Ships|Ion]] with two pulse lasers and two tons of cargo space,
and the galaxy holds 14,906 catalogued
systems — 5,340 of them
inside the height the map can reach — before the generator fills in everything
between them.

This wiki documents what the game does not tell you: what a scan is worth, what
an ore sells for, and what each [[Module Mods|module upgrade]] costs in
materials.

Everything is bought with '''credits''' (CR), and there are four ways to earn
them: [[Missions|station job boards]], [[Trading|trading]], [[Mining|mining]],
and [[Exploration|exploration]], which pays best of all once your ship can reach
the systems nobody has catalogued.

== The Story ==
Humanity has spread out from Sol into the '''Core Systems''', where androids now do
much of the work and the frontier mines resources for the rich. The United Empire and
the Trade Federation are not officially at war, but their cold war keeps turning hot,
and independent pilots like you are hired to do what neither side will own. Beyond the
explored stars, the [[Side quests|side quests]] hint at older, stranger things.

Your space station:
There is an '''abandoned station''' waiting in one of five systems, and once you
have repaired it, it is yours: a second base that stores cargo, sells it while
you are elsewhere, moves itself across the galaxy, and gets raided by pirates.
The game never tells you it exists.

Nothing marks it until you fly there: the station is created the moment you first

them are inside 90 ly of Sol, which is early-ship range.

Once you have seen it, the galaxy map's '''Filters''' screen grows a
'''Find own station''' button, next to Reset filters and Show journey. It
does not fly you anywhere: it scrolls the map to where the station is, which
matters later, because the station moves.

== Trading while you are away ==
Mark cargo in the store '''for sale''' and the station finds its own buyers:
every station inside the Trade Port's range that wants that good. What they pay
depends on how badly they want it — '''×1.2''' at neutral demand, '''×1.4''' at
high demand — plus the Trade Port's percentage. Only the best buyer for each good
is kept.

A sale happens '''every 30 seconds of play, and only while you are not in the
station's system'''. Each one moves one good to one buyer, and the size of the
batch is a roll:

{| class="fandom-table sortable"
! Chance !! Tons sold
|-
| 30% || 8–20
|-
| 30% || 30–80
|-
| 20% || 100–160
|-
| 20% || 170–250
|}

The money is '''tons × base price × 1,000 × demand''', the same arithmetic as
selling it yourself, so the station earns most when it is holding something
expensive. See [[Trading]] for what each good is worth.

== Pirates ==
Once the store holds more than '''50 tons''', pirates start arriving: the game
checks every '''10 minutes''' of play.

'''If you are there''', they hail you and name a price. Pay and they leave.
Refuse and you fight up to '''five''' ships, matched to your own hull and at the
game's highest danger level. Your guards fight alongside you.

'''If you are away''', it is settled without you. Every guard's weapons are added
up — damage times rate of fire — against a raid worth 50 to 150, the damage is
shared out, and a guard that survives gains experience that makes it tougher next
time. '''If every guard is destroyed the pirates empty the store''' and leave the
station 10–13% damaged, which is ore out of your hold again.

Guards are ships from your own fleet, parked at the station, so the real cost of
protecting it is a hull you are not flying — and repairing a damaged guard is
charged to you.

== Moving it ==
The Warp drive subsystem moves the whole station to any system inside its range,
paid for in materials. One rule: '''it cannot jump to a system that already has a
station'''. That is what makes where you park it a decision — in reach of several
stations it sells faster, but the pirates know where it is either way.

Its appearance can be changed for '''10,000,000 CR''', which is cosmetic only and
takes effect the next time you arrive.
Getting started:
You start in an '''Ion''' with two basic pulse lasers, a basic shield and a cargo
rack that holds two tons. After the tutorial you are offered a job in the '''Ross
720''' system, and your starter ship cannot get there. That gap is the game's
opening problem.

Tap your ship, a station or a planet to open its menu. [[Game Interface]] lists
what every button does.

== Your first credits ==
Take item transport missions from any station within warp reach. One to two tons
of cargo pays '''50,000–60,000 CR''', and finishing jobs also earns influence
with the [[Factions|faction]] that owns the station, which unlocks better-paid
work later.

Spend the first profits on cargo racks so you can carry more per run, and learn
your way around the [https://galaxy-genome.github.io/map/?system=Sol Core Systems] while you are
limited to them.

== Your second ship ==
The '''Phoenix''' is the usual first upgrade: a well-rounded multipurpose hull
with a warp drive that widens your range considerably. Its hull is about three
times the strength of the Chaser, so it survives the transport and courier work
that pays for it. The '''Chaser''' suits easy to moderate combat instead.

== Then explore ==
Exploration is the fastest money in the game by a wide margin. See [[Exploration]].

Two cautions before you go far:
* You are not paid for discoveries until you reach a station and sell them from its '''Discoveries''' menu.
* Deep space has no repairs and no fuel but what you scoop. See [[Modules#Fuel tanks and scooping|fuel]].

=== Picking up cargo ===
''"In order to pick up any cargo, you need to open onboard menu and find it in the
"Objects" panel on the first tab."'' Each line reads '''Cargo''' or
'''Material''', the amount in brackets, then what it is. Tap the line and the
autopilot flies onto it. ''"Before picking up the cargo, make sure that there is
enough space on your ship for it."''

=== Fleet ===
The Fleet screen sets how your mercenaries fight under '''Mode''':
* '''Defensive mode''': ''"mercenaries will only attack ships that attack your ship or mercenary ships."''
* '''Attack mode''': ''"allows mercenaries to attack any target you choose."'' They also go after your target when your weapons are out.

Each goes for the nearest such ship. '''Repair''' on one ship, or '''Repair all
ships''', repairs and reloads ammunition for the price shown, but
''"The button for repairing mercenary ships will only work near the station."''
A ship further than 40 light seconds from a station gets ''"Too long distance
between the selected ship and nearest station."''

Exploration:
Finding new worlds pays, and you are paid '''every time''' you find one, not only
the first time anyone did. You need a '''Planet Scanner''' fitted. You collect by
selling at a station's '''Discoveries''' menu, which also earns reputation with
that station and with the [[Factions|faction]] that owns it.

== How a discovery actually happens ==
[[File:Planet menu.png|thumb|The planet menu. Scan starts a scan by hand]]
Mostly it happens '''by flying near the thing'''. Any planet that comes within
your scanner's range is discovered automatically, a green '''+ CR''' message
appears, and the value is banked until you sell it at a station.

Two things follow from that:
* '''Stars are free.''' They are discovered as soon as you arrive in the system, at any distance, and some of them are worth a fortune. See below.
* '''Asteroid belts do not count.''' They are excluded from the tally entirely.

You can also scan a planet by hand: tap it and choose '''Scan''' from the
[[Game Interface#Planet Menu|planet menu]]. ''"When scanning the surface of the
planet, the cost of research data doubles."'' A scan banks the planet's value a
second time, on top of what discovering it paid.

Each system shows a '''mapped / total''' count, so you can see what is left
before moving on. Your ship's '''Specs → Stars and Planets''' list shows every
object type, what it pays, how rare it is, and whether you have found one yet.

== The Spectrum Analyzer ==
The Planet Scanner discovers planets; the '''Spectrum Analyzer''' shows you where
they are. ''"If it is absent on the ship, then unknown planets will not be visible
on the system map, so this module is necessary in space exploration."'' It has to
be fitted and powered for the system map to draw planets you have not found yet.

Its panel shows the spectrum of the bodies around you, and choosing a wavelength
narrows the search: ''"When a specific wavelength is selected, the signal around
your ship will point towards planets that have a spectrum with an absorption line
on the selected wavelength. Thanks to that, you can discover only the most
valuable planets."'' The panel lists the elements that absorb at the chosen
wavelength, and the signal points to planets with any of them in their surface or
atmosphere. The panel will not open below 70% condition.

== Neutron stars and black holes ==
Pulsars, magnetars, Quark stars and black holes pull your ship in
once you are close. A '''HIGH GRAVITY''' warning appears, the pull is stronger
with your engines off, and close in at a near standstill it damages the hull as
well as heating it. ''"Having fallen into such a trap, it's important to keep
calm and first redistribute the power to engines."''

== Space storms ==
''"A fairly common anomaly that occurs near flying clouds around hot stars.
Lightning strikes can produce damage to the electronics of the spaceship and lead
to the hull's overheating."'' A storm can only form where the system's main star
is an A, B or O star, a giant, a Wolf-Rayet star, a white dwarf, a Herbig star, a
neutron star or a black hole, and strikes come only where the storm clouds show.
A strike comes every 3 to 12 seconds, heats the ship, and takes 2.5% to 5% of
the integrity of one module at random. The game's advice: ''"It is recommended to
carry a repair module and heat sinks in case of long-range missions."'' See
[[Modules#Repair Module|Repair Module]].

== The Planet Scanner ==
Range is the whole point of the module: a longer scanner discovers planets from
further out, so you fly less to clear the same system.

{| class="fandom-table sortable"
! Scanner !! Grade !! Range !! Power !! Mass !! Cost (CR)
|-
| 1D || D || 230 || 0.2 || 0 || 1,000
|-
| 1C || C || 270 || 0.3 || 0 || 12,000
|-
| 1B || B || 320 || 0.4 || 0 || 50,000
|-
| 1A || A || 390 || 0.35 || 0 || 350,000
|}

Every grade is '''massless''', so a scanner never costs you jump range. Note that
'''A draws less power than B''' as well as reaching 70 further, so B is worth
skipping if you can afford to wait.

=== What each grade is actually worth ===
Range is measured in '''light seconds''', the same unit a planet's orbit is in,
and the innermost orbit a system can hold is 65. So a scanner's range is exactly
the question ''how much of this system do I get for free''.

Across the '''4,116''' catalogued systems that pay anything at all, this is
what each grade banks on arrival, before you fly anywhere:

{| class="fandom-table sortable"
! Scanner !! Cost (CR) !! Mean banked on arrival (CR) !! Gained over the grade below (CR) !! Systems to pay it back
|-
| none || — || 39,503 || — || —
|-
| 1D || 1,000 || 64,328 || 24,825 || under 1
|-
| 1C || 12,000 || 69,549 || 5,221 || 3
|-
| 1B || 50,000 || 75,433 || 5,884 || 7
|-
| 1A || 350,000 || 81,782 || 6,349 || 48
|}

'''The 1D is the best purchase in the game.''' One thousand credits takes the
average system from 39,503 CR to 64,328 CR banked for
turning up, and it pays for itself in the first system you visit. Nothing else in
the outfitter does that.

After that the returns fall off a cliff. Each grade above it adds roughly
5,221 to 6,349 CR a system, for eleven thousand,
thirty-eight thousand and three hundred thousand credits in turn. The 1A takes
48 systems to break even. They all pay back eventually if you
explore seriously; none of them is urgent.

== You cannot scan near Sol ==
Within '''300 ly of Sol''' every body is treated as already explored:
the scan is refused and nothing is paid. The system tooltip says so outright,
''Explored: yes''. This is why scanning is not something you can do on your
doorstep, and why a scanner is a purchase for when you can already travel. A
couple of objects are exceptions; see [[Spoilers]].

'''There is a second one.''' The same rule applies within '''150 ly of
The Void''', which is easy to be caught out by: it sits over 4,500 ly from Sol, so
you arrive after a long trip expecting untouched sky and find everything already
surveyed. The rule is per system and covers '''stars as well as planets''', so
there is nothing left to sell.

'''The star is the reason to go and the planets are why you stay.''' A bright star
is visible on the map before you arrive and pays the moment you drop in. Several
of these systems carry more value in planets than in the star itself, and those
planets have to be flown to one at a time.

That is what the '''Banked on arrival''' and '''Hops''' columns are for. Arrival
is what a ship with a 1D scanner collects for turning up, with no flying at all;
a hop is one body worth crossing the system for, which in practice is a minute of
autopilot and two minutes of menus. A system with a large total and no hops is a
better trip than one with a larger total and three.

== Reading the table ==
* '''Water Giants''' and '''Earth Like Planets''' pay the most, and both are rare.
* '''Ice Planets''' are common and pay 1,500 CR.
* The game's own '''Stars and planets''' table shows some types as a range, such as 1,700-90,000 CR for a '''Rock Planet'''. The upper figure is for a planet in the habitable zone, and no type that displays a range can ever qualify for it: the test is against the type's whole temperature band, and every one of those bands falls partly outside it. What you are paid is the lower figure, every time.
* Scan value is per object, so a system is worth the sum of its planets. A system of four gas giants can beat one with more bodies in it.

Finding an '''Earth Like Planet''' or an '''Ammonia Planet''' for the first time
each unlocks an achievement, as do two of the rarest [[The galaxy#Star types|stars]].

The [https://galaxy-genome.github.io/map/ Galaxy Genome Map] filters on either figure — total value, or what
your own scanner banks on arrival — and systems the game already counts as
''explored'' score zero, so they never appear on either list.

Factions:
Five factions hold the settled galaxy between them. Which one likes you decides
which [[Ships|ships]] you may buy and which [[Side quests|side quests]] you are
offered.

== Reputation is the sum of your stations ==
There is no separate faction score to grind. '''Your standing with a faction is
the total of your reputations at its individual stations.''' Do well at one
United Empire station and the United Empire as a whole thinks better of you; the
faction number is just addition.

Two things follow from that.

'''A faction with more stations is easier to climb.''' Every station is more
headroom, and the factions are not evenly sized.

Reputation and ranks:
Three separate things track your progress, and they do not feed each other. It is
worth knowing which one a given activity pays into, because the size of the
reward differs enormously between them.

== Station and faction reputation ==
Earned by completing [[Missions|missions]] and by selling
[[Exploration|discoveries]] at a station.

* '''Station reputation''' decides what that station's mission board pays you. It has a ceiling: ''"Reputation at each station is limited to 100 units."'' Allied is as high as one station's standing goes.
* '''Faction reputation''' is the sum of your standing at that faction's stations, which the game's help calls '''influence points'''. It decides which [[Ships|ships]] you are allowed to buy, and some [[Side quests|side quests]] ask for a minimum of it before they will start: ''"Influence points are needed to access some ship models and side quests that are related to certain factions."''

This is the big one. A mission's reward is its base value raised to the power of
your standing, so the same job pays '''17 times more''' at Allied than at Neutral:

{| class="fandom-table sortable"
! Standing !! A Mining contract pays
|-
| Neutral || 180,000
|-
| Confiding || 468,000
|-
| Friendly || 1,216,800
|-
| Allied || 3,163,680
|}

Working one station until it trusts you beats taking the best-looking job at a
station that does not.

== Exploration rank ==
Earned by '''selling discoveries''' and by completing '''Transport''' (tourist)
[[Missions|missions]], and measured by the credits you have made from both in
total. A Transport mission's reward counts toward it in full. It adds a flat
percentage to what discoveries sell for.

== Combat rank ==
Earned by fighting, and measured the same way. It adds the same percentage to
bounty payouts, '''and it is what lets you own a fleet''': wingman ships that fly
with you, capped in both number and price by your rank.

The fleet is hired, not free: ''"They take a certain percentage of the money
you earn."'' Each mercenary takes a share, and the fleet screen shows the total.
It comes off mission rewards, bounties and side quest rewards, and the total
never exceeds '''90%'''.

Both top out at '''+18%''', and the two ladders differ at exactly one rung:
Trailblazer gives '''+8%''' where Expert gives '''+6%'''. Next to reputation's
multiplier these are small, so neither rank is a reason to grind on its own. The
fleet is.

== Trading rank ==
There is a '''third''' ladder, easy to miss because nothing points at it. It runs
on what you have earned by [[Trading|trade]], and it has its own nine names:

''Penniless · Mostly Penniless · Penniless Peddler · Dealer · Merchant · Broker · Entrepreneur · Tycoon · Prime''

It shares the top rung, '''Prime''', with the other two. Earning all three at once
is what the '''Absolute Prime''' [[Achievements|achievement]] asks for.

Trading rank also sets the size of some [[Events and Tasks|Daily Tasks]]: Mining
Rush and Illegal Trader both scale their target count off it, so a high trading
rank makes those dailies longer as well as more valuable.

== Karma ==
Karma is not a rank you earn, it is a record of how you behave, and the game
gives it names too:

''Despised · Disliked · Average · Liked · Revered''

To see yours, tap your ship and choose '''Missions''' ([[Game Interface#Ship Menu|ship menu]]). That screen is
available whenever your ship is stationary, and shows your karma level and points above your
[[Reputation and ranks|faction reputation]]. Karma is one number for the whole
galaxy, not a standing with each faction.

[[File:Karma on the Missions screen.png|thumb|Karma on the Missions screen]]

It moves both ways. Clearing pirate activity from a system is worth
'''+2'''; destroying law enforcement costs you. It matters because
[[Side quests|side quests]] check it in '''both directions''' — some will not
talk to you until your record is clean, and others will not talk to you unless it
is dirty. A spotless record closes doors as surely as a bad one.

Mission boards check it too: ''"Too high karma will block access to quests in
systems with anarchy... too low a karma value will prevent you from accepting
quests in high security systems."'' A board that turns you away says ''"You are
not trusted."'' and offers nothing:

|-
| In a High security system || Despised
|-
| Pirate || Liked or Revered
|}
Stations:
There are '''156''' stations. A station is where you sell
[[Exploration|discoveries]], take [[Missions|missions]], buy [[Modules|modules]] and
[[Ships|ships]], and repair. Generated systems never have one, so stations are
the fixed points the rest of the galaxy hangs off.

[[File:Station menu.png|thumb|The station menu]]
Tap a station to open its menu. [[Game Interface#Station Menu|Game Interface]]
lists what each button does.

One station is not on any of these lists: there is an abandoned one waiting to be
repaired, and it becomes yours. See [[Your space station]].

What a station sells depends on its '''type''', so a run for a specific module
means finding the right kind of station rather than the nearest one.

'''The game never labels a station with its type.''' Click a system and you get a
name, a faction and a distance, and nothing else until you open its menu. The station's
'''name''' is the only handle you have, which is what the table below is for, and
what the [[Galaxy Genome Map|map]] puts in its tooltip.

Worse, '''the names do not describe the stock'''. A Trading station carries the
industrial list; an Industrial station carries the trade-post list. Read the
Purpose column, not the Type column.

Mining:
Asteroids are broken up for ore and the pieces collected into your hold. You need
a mining weapon fitted and free cargo space to hold what you cut loose. Ore is
sold at any station's market.

Most systems have at least one asteroid belt, and '''every belt holds three
ores''' in fixed proportions, decided when the system was made. A belt listed at
50% Painite yields Painite about half the time you mine it, and it will still do
so next month.

== The equipment ==

=== Mining Laser ===
The ordinary way in. ''"Allows to extract minerals and metals from asteroids.
Activated automatically when you tap and hold the asteroid down."'' Hold on a rock
and it cuts; anything it frees drifts loose for you to collect.

''"The more modules like "mining laser" installed on your ship, the faster
mining."'' Each laser's hit closes part of the gap to a finished cut, so every
extra laser helps and each one adds less. ''"After the ore breaks off from the
asteroid, it will be displayed on the panel of nearby objects. By pressing the
button of the nearest object, your ship will automatically collect ore."'' The
panel lists what floats nearby, closest first; tap a line and the ship flies onto
it. Touching the engine controls takes the ship back.

'''Pirates come for miners.''' ''"Beware of pirates who hunt mining ships.
Periodically change the area in which you mine ore."'' The game counts the time
you spend mining in a system and sends a pirate each time it passes a mark. The
first comes after 2 to 3 minutes in Anarchy, in a Conflict Zone and in a system
without stations short of deep space, 2 to 4 in Low security, 3 to 7 in Medium
and 3 to 8 in High, and more keep coming while you stay. The count starts
again in each new system. In deep space no pirate is sent.

=== Spectrum Analyzer ===
''"Activate the spectrometer while in the asteroid belt to see the types of ore
located there."'' Inside a belt, the '''Spectrum Analyzer''' panel reads
'''ASTEROID BELT''' and lists the belt's three ores with the share of each, so
you can check a belt before you start cutting.

=== Seismic charges ===
A launcher that ''"destroys the integrity of asteroids, allowing access to more
valuable resources."'' Some asteroids hold '''deep materials''' that a laser
cannot reach; charges crack them open. Any ship that has a slot for them can
carry them. What they uncover is described under [[Mining#Deep materials|Deep materials]].

=== The Miner ability ===
Two ships, the '''Delver''' and the '''Grinder''', carry an ability the shop
lists as '''Miner'''. While you are in attack mode it '''recolours every asteroid
that holds deep materials''', so you can see at a glance which rocks are worth
spending a charge on instead of testing them one by one.

=== Collector Drone Controller ===

==== Drones are cargo, and they can be lost ====
A drone is an item in your hold, not part of the module. Launching one frees a
slot when it comes back, so the controller is never used up. The '''drone''' can
be, in two ways:

* It is '''damaged''' on the way and does not return.
* It returns and '''your hold is full''', so there is nowhere to put it. The game says ''"No space for drone"'' and the drone is gone.

That second one catches people out. Filling your hold with ore is exactly when
your drones are most likely to die, so leave room for them to come home.

== Deep materials ==
The two most valuable ores never show up when you scan a belt. '''Void Opal'''
(600 CR a ton) and
'''Musgravite''' (400 CR) sit
inside a few asteroids, out of reach of a mining laser.

* '''Only some systems have them.''' About one belt system in ten holds Void Opal, and about one in ten Musgravite. No system has both, and a system without either has no deep materials at all. Which one a system holds never changes.
* '''You need a belt.''' Deep materials are inside a belt's asteroids.
* '''Roughly one asteroid in twenty''' in those systems holds them, '''3 to 6 tons''' each.
* '''Crack them with [[Mining#Seismic charges|Seismic charges]].''' A laser cannot reach deep materials.
* '''The [[Mining#The Miner ability|Miner ability]]''' on the Delver and Grinder recolours the asteroids that hold them, so charges go where they pay.
* '''No contract asks for them.''' Mining missions only ever name the belt ores.

The [[Galaxy Genome Map]] finds them: pick either in '''Ore present'''.

* [https://galaxy-genome.github.io/map/?ore=VoidOpal Systems with Void Opal]
* [https://galaxy-genome.github.io/map/?ore=Musgravite Systems with Musgravite]

== Mining for contracts ==
Stations post '''Mining''' missions asking for a set tonnage of one ore, with
'''12 hours''' to deliver, which suits a belt you already know. The ore is always
a belt ore, never Void Opal or Musgravite.

What they pay depends almost entirely on your standing at that station. The same
contract runs from '''180,000 CR''' as a stranger to over '''3,000,000 CR''' once you
are Allied there. See [[Missions]].

== Finding a belt worth the trip ==
Checking systems one at a time is slow. The [[Galaxy Genome Map]] filters by ore
and by minimum percentage, so you can ask for
[https://galaxy-genome.github.io/map/?ore=Painite&pct=40 belts at least 40% Painite] and route to the nearest.
Trading:
Every station has a market. Buy a commodity where it is cheap, carry it somewhere
it is not, and keep the difference. Nothing shoots at you, and unlike
[[Exploration|scanning]] it pays from the first hour.

The whole of it comes down to one number: '''how many tons you can carry'''.
Everything else is arithmetic you can do in advance, and this page does it.

== How a price is made ==
A station quotes '''1,000 CR a ton''' times the commodity's base
price, moved by two things and nothing else.

'''The demand tier.''' Each market type a station carries is ranked, and the
rank sets the multiplier. The game shows it as ''Demand'' in the market list and
as a ''Profit'' percentage on the trade screen.

{| class="fandom-table sortable"
! Demand !! It sells to you at !! It buys from you at
|-
| highest || x0.76 || x1.24
|-
| second || x0.84 || x1.16
|-
| rest || x0.92 || x1.08
|-
| neutral || — || x1.00 exactly
|}

'''Your trader rank.''' The bonus is subtracted from what you pay and added to
what you are paid, so it counts twice.

'''The market list is colour-coded by tier.''' ''"Items in abundance are
highlighted in green and items that are out of stock are highlighted in red.
Green items are sold at a price below average. Red items are bought at a price
above average."'' Green lines are what the station sells, at one of the three
selling tiers. Red lines are what it buys at a premium, and it has none of them to
sell you. Blue lines it buys at the neutral price.

At the best tier on both ends that makes the margin
'''48% of base price''' at your first rank and
'''68%''' at your last. At the worst tier
it is only 16% — so the same run can be worth
three times as much depending on which lines the two stations happened to roll.

== Your hold is the only limit ==
'''Prices do not move when you trade.''' A station's price for a line is fixed
by its base price, its demand tier and your trader rank, and selling a full hold
pays the same per ton as selling one. The market generator computes a stock
figure for every line and '''nothing ever reads it''': no station runs out, and
no station refuses a full load. What caps a transaction is the free space in
your hold and the credits in your account.

That makes the strategy simple to state: '''carry the most expensive thing on
offer'''. A ton is a ton, so the margin per ton is the base price times the
spread, and the ranking below never changes.

== Profit per jump ==
Distance does not enter the price, so a run earns the same margin whether the
two stations are one jump apart or ten. What distance costs is time and fuel:

* profit per jump = tons carried × margin per ton ÷ jumps between the two stations

A 64-ton hold of Hafnium at the best tiers earns
95,232 CR a trip, whether that trip
is one jump or four; per jump, the four-jump run earns a quarter as much.
'''The nearest matching pair of stations pays the most per jump.'''

== Pirates on the way in ==
''"Be careful when transporting cargo in systems with low security, avoid direct
routes from the star to the station, as you may encounter pirates."'' Ships that
appear in a system with stations, pirates among them, are placed on the straight
line from the star to a station and fly along it to the station. Pirates are
commonest in Conflict Zones, then Anarchy, then Low security.

== The market rotates ==
Every station is dealt '''three market types''': one it sells, one it buys at a
premium, one it buys at the neutral price. They come from a single rotating index
that walks the whole station list, so no two neighbours are dealt the same hand.
Within each hand, which line gets the top demand tier, which the second and
which the rest is shuffled too.

Both turn over together on one '''market counter''', every '''4,000''' on it. The
counter goes up:
* by '''1 each second''' you play, once the tutorial is past the step where you change a module's power priority, so about every 67 minutes with no trading at all;
* by '''3 for each ton you sell''' at a station other than the one you last bought at. Buying adds nothing;
* by '''1 for each unit''' handed over for a goods mission.

So heavy trading turns the markets over sooner.

The consequence is that '''a station's stock is not a property of the station'''.
Come back later and it is selling something else. The game's own galaxy map has an
''Availability of Goods'' filter that shows the current state; the
[[Galaxy Genome Map|map here]] shows the parts that never change, which the game
never tells you at all.

Two market types are never dealt out:
* '''Minerals''' are removed from every station's selling and neutral-buying hands, so they can only ever be sold to a station, never bought from one.
* '''Other''' is not in the rotation at all. It has exactly one buyer, below.

=== Getting caught ===
Law enforcement scans you whenever you carry Slaves or Tretonin, or cargo for an
illegal job from a station bar. The scan takes '''4 seconds'''
(''SCAN DETECTED! [1/4 s]''), and '''Silent Mode''' stops it. What happens when
it completes depends on what it finds.

'''Slaves or Tretonin''' have no way out: ''"Drop illegal cargo, otherwise you
will be destroyed!"'' You lose '''3 karma''', the system fines you '''500 CR a
ton''' of the two, and the law ship attacks.

'''Cargo for a bar job''' gets a choice: ''"No cargo shipping records found.
Provide permission to transport cargo."''
* '''Show fake documents''' is a coin flip. Win and the job's cargo is made legal. Lose and you pay '''800 CR a ton''' in fines in that system and '''3 karma'''.
* '''Run away''' costs '''500 CR a ton''' and no karma, and the law ship turns on you: ''"This is disobedience to the guardians of the system. You will be destroyed!"''

Fines are held against the '''system''', not against you globally, so an unpaid
fine closes that system's services until you settle it. See
[[Combat#Bounties and fines|Combat]].

'''Buying and selling are not watched.''' A station never checks your hold, so
the risk is only in flight between the two.

== Your own station ==
A repaired [[Spoilers|space station]] of your own trades without you. List cargo
for sale, and it finds stations within its trade range that buy that market type,
taking the best one per commodity:

* '''x1.2''' where the buyer wants it at the neutral price
* '''x1.4''' where the buyer wants it at the premium

That x1.4 is better than the x1.24 you can get in person, so anything
your station can sell is worth listing rather than hauling. Upgrading the Trade
Port raises both the range and the profit.
Missions:
Missions are the backbone of income at every stage, not just the early one. Every
[[Stations|station]] has a board, under '''Missions''' in the
[[Game Interface#Station Menu|station menu]], and each job pays some mix of '''credits''',
'''materials''' and '''[[Reputation and ranks|reputation]]''' with that station and its
[[Factions|faction]].

Three things will stop you accepting one: not enough free cargo space, not enough
credits for the cargo insurance, or too many missions already active.

You can give up an active mission from the '''Missions''' screen of the
[[Game Interface#Ship Menu|ship menu]]: tap it and choose '''Decline'''. ''"Do you
want to decline it (your reputation will be decreased)?"'' Declining costs the
same station reputation as failing it.

== Reputation multiplies the reward ==
This is the single most important thing about missions. A job's payout is its
base reward raised by your '''standing at that station''', and the step between
tiers is a multiplication, not an addition:

Working one station until you are trusted there beats taking the first job you

It scales worse than anything else, 1.5x a tier against 2.6x for the best jobs, and most Courier cards are '''fixed at Neutral''' whatever your standing, because the generator uses them to guarantee low-tier work is always on the board. Those pay exactly 10,000 CR for ever. The ones that do roll a tier reach 33,750 at Allied, which is still the worst on the board.
* '''Deliver''' — buy a named good and take it to a named station. You supply the cargo, so you need the hold space and the credits up front.
* '''Station needs''' — the same trade inward: bring a named good back to the station offering the job. The quantity is '''(tier + 1) squared, times 2 to 5''' units, so the same job at Ally asks for several times what it asks at Low.
* '''Mining rush''' — mine a named mineral and bring it back. The tier is set by the mineral rather than by you: the cheap ores are Low jobs and anything at or above a basic cost of 1 is a Very High one, which is why the board pays so much better once you can work the rare belts. Never fewer than 2 units, and never [[Mining#Deep materials|Void Opal or Musgravite]]. See [[Mining]].
* '''Donation''' — you pay the station rather than being paid. The reward figure is applied to your balance as a '''negative''', and what you get back is [[Reputation and ranks|reputation]] with that station and its [[Factions|faction]]. Nothing to fly to and nothing to carry: it is reputation bought with credits.
* '''Transport''' — carry a passenger to a system '''100 ly per tier''' away, up to 400 at Very High. The pay is the base scaled by how far you actually went against that target, so the long runs pay disproportionately. A hundred hours on the clock. On arrival the passenger asks to go back, and offers two answers. '''Let's go back''' completes the job, and it pays when you return to the station that issued it. '''Throw a tourist into space''' fails the mission and jettisons the passenger in an escape pod. Completing one also raises your [[Reputation and ranks#Exploration rank|exploration rank]].
* '''Rescue Mission''' — the best-paying job in the game. A named ship is stranded in a distant system, out of fuel or badly damaged, and wants what you carry. The distance model and the hundred-hour limit match Transport.
* '''Take down pirate''' — destroy a named pirate ship in a system within 15 ly. What you are sent against is set by the tier, from an Ion at Low to a Goliath or a Reaper at Very High. Three hulls carry '''1,600,000 CR''' on top of the reward, Hyperion, Reaper and Discordia, and a Nemesis carries 400,000. See [[Combat]].
* '''Elimination''' — the same fight against a target who is not a pirate, at a station of another faction. Same hulls, same bonuses.
* '''Alien Hunt''' — an Angler mother and her brood, in a system within 100 ly. One fixed danger level whatever your standing, so the tier changes the pay and nothing else.
* '''Robbery''' — destroy a hauler and take its cargo. Never offered at Low.
* '''Intimidate''' — frighten a captain rather than kill him, and that distinction is the whole job.

=== Robbery ===
* The target is a named freighter with an escort, and the cargo is always one of six: Battle Weapons, Basic Medicines, Nano Medicines, Robotics, Natural Fabrics or Leather.
* Bring back '''15 units per tier''', plus up to 4 more.
* A Hyperion, Reaper or Discordia target carries far more, and the quantity asked of you rises with it.
* The hold space has to be free before the cargo drops, or you cannot collect it.

=== Intimidate ===
* Kill the escort first: one ship at Low and Medium, two at High, more above.
* Then damage the named target until its hull is '''under 30%''' and stop.
* It surrenders, the mission completes, and it flies away.
* '''Destroying it fails the mission.''' There is no partial credit.

=== The rare boards ===
At any station within '''100 ly of Sol''', each board refresh has a '''1 in 20'''
chance of carrying one of three jobs that pay orders of magnitude more than
anything else, and that '''never expire''':

* A Courier job to '''[https://galaxy-genome.github.io/map/?system=Lone%20Star&station=Laickoms%20Station Laickoms Station]''', 12,000,000 CR and up.
* A Courier job to '''[https://galaxy-genome.github.io/map/?system=J3571&station=Astro%20City Astro City]''', 5,600,000 CR and up.
* A Transport run to '''[https://galaxy-genome.github.io/map/?system=Sagittarius%20A%2A Sagittarius A*]''', 30,000,000 CR and up.

All three are offered at Confiding, so they are reachable early. Checking the
boards around Sol is worth the detour on its own:
[https://galaxy-genome.github.io/map/?filters=station&lymax=100 every station inside 100 ly].

Station needs, Mining rush, Deliver and Robbery take the goods out of your hold
on completion and count the payout toward your [[Trading#Trader rank|trader
rank]], so they are trade jobs as much as they are missions.

== Reading the board ==
* '''Courier''' and '''Deliver''' are where you start. Short timers, small cargo, no combat. Courier scales the worst of anything on the board, so leave it behind.
* '''Mining''' and '''Station needs''' give you twelve hours, enough to fly somewhere specific and return. See [[Mining]].
* '''Transport''' and '''Rescue Mission''' allow a hundred hours and pay the most. Tourist runs are capped separately, so you cannot fill the board with them.
* The combat jobs, '''Take down pirate''', '''Elimination''', '''Robbery''' and '''Alien Hunt''', want a ship that can fight before you accept one.

Missions expire. The timer runs whether or not you are flying toward them.
Combat:
Combat is where the late game money is: bounties, pirate contracts, and the
'''fleet''' that [[Reputation and ranks|combat rank]] eventually unlocks. It is
also the fastest way to lose a ship you spent hours paying for.

== Attack mode ==
Putting your cannons out changes how your ship behaves, and the game will tell
you so:

* ''"Speed limit: turn off cannons"'' — you are slower with weapons deployed.
* ''"WARP ERROR: TURN OFF CANNONS"'' — you cannot jump until you stow them.

So you cannot flee a fight by warping out until you have disengaged first. Decide
before you commit.

Warping out is still a way to escape: ''"There is nothing wrong with going into
the warp to get away from the chase. At the same time, the preparation time for a
warp jump can be increased."'' The countdown is '''5 seconds''', and '''45''' when
a ship targeting you within 300 light seconds is at least as heavy as yours. To
last that long, the game says to ''"use protection systems (chaff launcher and
defense turret), turn on the silent mode"''.

=== Running ===
Outrunning a fight is the other way out, and three rules decide it:
* '''Engine pips raise top speed''': x1.1, x1.2 and x1.3 at 2, 3 and 4 pips.
* '''The afterburner's extra speed is cut to a third''' while your weapons are out, or while a ship at least as heavy as yours is targeting you within 300 light seconds. Past that speed the ship is braked back.
* '''NPCs give up at 300 light seconds''' (below), and they never retreat on their own, so distance is the only thing that ends a chase you cannot win.

So stow the weapons before you run. They slow you, and they keep you from
jumping.

'''Range is the constraint people underrate.''' A Fragment Cannon reaches 8 and a
Torpedo reaches 45 — nearly six times as far. A loadout that mixes them wastes
one of them in any given fight, because you cannot be at both ranges at once.

'''Shot speed decides whether you can hit anything.''' A Beam Laser and an Energy
Lance arrive instantly at 3,000. A Plasma Cannon or a Torpedo travels at 400 or
200, which against a moving target at long range means leading it badly or
missing. Slow and heavy only pays against something large or stationary.

'''Ammo cost is a running bill.''' Lasers and the Gauss Gun cost nothing per shot.
A Torpedo costs 50 and a Mine 75, so those are weapons you spend rather than
fire.

'''Power is the other running bill.''' Every weapon draws on the weapons pool
while it fires, and ''"Installing energy cannons alone will quickly deplete the
capacitor charge and you will fire intermittently."'' At class 2 a Beam Laser
draws 1.5 a second and a Plasma Cannon 2, against 0.34 for a Cannon. The game's
advice is to ''"Combine energy cannons with kinetic cannons or
missiles/torpedoes."'' See [[Ship stats#Weapons draw|Ship stats]].

How to read it:
* '''Every hit is cut by a quarter''' before anything else, for you and for NPCs alike. The two damage columns already include that.
* '''Hits per second is what you can keep up.''' The Cannon fires 4 a second but empties its 48-round clip in 12 seconds and takes 3 to reload. The Fragment Cannon fires its three 12-pellet bursts almost at once, then reloads for 8 seconds, so it does its damage in one close pass. Mines drop three at a time and re-arm 5 seconds after the last.
* '''Power per shot''' comes out of the weapons pool. When the pool holds less than one shot's worth, that weapon does not fire.
* '''Heat per shot''' is multiplied by your hull's weapon heat factor. Missiles, Torpedoes and Mines add no heat at all.
* '''Plasma Cannon and Gauss Gun hits on a bare hull also damage a random module''', and explosions damage one too. Lasers and the Energy Lance heat the target: a third of the weapon's heat per shot while its shields hold, two thirds once they are down.
* '''Worn weapons jam.''' Every shot wears the weapon a little. Below 10% integrity it stops, and below 40% it can jam at random.

=== The Railgun is the safe default ===
It ''"inflicts both thermal and kinetic damage"'' and '''partially passes through
shields''', which means it is the one weapon that never has a bad matchup. Every
other choice is a bet on what you will meet: thermal strips shields and struggles
with armour, kinetic does the reverse. Carrying a Railgun is how you stop
guessing, at the price of never being the best answer to anything.

It is sold at '''HiTech''' stations only.

== Damage types ==
Where a hit lands depends on its type and on whether the target's shields are
still up. Each figure multiplies the hit after the quarter is taken off:

* '''Damage past the last shield point is lost.''' The hit that breaks the shields does not carry over to the hull, and once broken they stay down until they recover above half, so everything lands on the hull in between.
* '''Only the Railgun and explosions reach the hull through shields.'''
* '''Once shields are down, the hull's armour counts.''' Hull damage is multiplied by 0.55 + 0.45 × 25 ÷ the ship's '''Armour Hardness''', so a ship rated 25 takes it in full, one rated 20 takes 11% more and one rated 80 takes 31% less. See [[Ship stats#Hull against damage types|Ship stats]].
* '''Systems pips cut shield damage''' to x0.9, x0.7 and x0.5 at 2, 3 and 4 pips.

=== Hull types ===
The hull module sets what the hull resists. A resistance takes its share off
every hull hit of that type; a Railgun hit on a bare hull is cut by both the
kinetic and the thermal figure, and Plasma and Gauss hits by the thermal one.

A '''Mirrored''' hull resists lasers, Plasma and Gauss; a '''Military''' hull

'''Picking weapons from this.''' Thermal, Plasma and Gauss strip shields at full
rate; kinetic and explosions break a bare hull at full rate. One of each covers
both halves of a fight.

== Shields, hull and heat ==
'''Shields''' absorb damage until they fail, then the '''hull''' takes it.

'''Heat''' is the resource that actually constrains a long fight. Firing builds
it, and a '''Shields Cell Bank''' recharges your shields fast at the cost of ''"an
increased heat load."'' A '''Heatsink Launcher''' ''"allows to reset ship heat in
a moment"'', which is the button that keeps you in a fight you would otherwise
have to break off. Those two pull against each other, and a fight that goes long
is usually decided by which one you pressed first.

== Unique abilities in a fight ==
Three ships fight in a way no amount of outfitting reproduces. All three are
top-tier faction hulls, so these are late-game answers to late-game problems, not
choices you make early. See [[Ships#Unique abilities|Ships]] for the full list.

=== Multi-target cannons fire ===
The '''Hyperion''' does not fire where you are looking. Every time
its guns cycle they pick a target at random from everything currently in range,
so a burst sprays across the whole group rather than concentrating on one hull.

'''That is a trade, not an upgrade.''' Against a pack of weak pirates it is
strictly better, because everything in the swarm is taking damage at once and
nothing gets to sit at full health. Against one heavy target it is strictly
worse, because you cannot make it focus. Choose the Hyperion for
the fights it suits and expect it to feel wrong in the others.

=== Big cannon ===
The '''Reaper''' is the only ship in the game with a '''class-5
weapon hardpoint'''. Everything else tops out at class 4, which means the Reaper
mounts a weapon nothing else can carry: the '''[[Combat#Weapons|Energy Lance]]'''.

The Lance is ''"an energy weapon that continuously emits a laser beam"'' dealing
thermal damage. The game adds that ''"the longer the beam continues, the more
damage is dealt"''; in play each beam deals the same damage once, one beam a
second, with the longest reach of any energy weapon. It comes in classes 2 through 4 as well, so smaller ships can carry one; only the
5D fits the Reaper's big mount. It is sold at '''HiTech''' stations.

How the wing behaves:
* '''One button launches them all''' (''"Fighters Launched"''), and pressing it again calls them back (''"Fighters Call Back"''). The hangar must be powered and above 70% integrity.

* They stay close. A fighter that strays too far from you breaks off and returns.

hull and shields, but each Vortex lost costs 90,000 CR to replace.


== Rating battles ==
The game's arena. You take on a fixed ladder of opponents one at a time, and the
game calls it '''Rating battles''' wherever it names it.

'''83''' levels. The prize rises by a flat 10,000 CR a rung:

 reward = 80,000 + (level - 1) x 10,000

So level 1 pays 80,000 CR and level 83 pays
900,000 CR. Clearing the whole ladder is
'''40,670,000 CR'''.

=== Why it matters beyond the money ===
'''Rating battles gate the [[Spoilers#The Warp Drive Booster|Warp Drive Booster]]''', the only module
that extends jump range past what a drive alone gives. It unlocks at
'''level 60''', by which point the ladder has paid out
22,500,000 CR.

There is a second route that skips the fighting entirely; see
[[Spoilers#The Warp Drive Booster|Spoilers]].

Winning level 77, the last against human pilots, is half of
unlocking the '''Shadow jump module'''; the other half is a side quest chain. See
[[Modules#How to get one|Modules]].

== Bounties and fines ==
Kills on wanted ships produce '''bounty claims''', which you cash at a station
like [[Exploration|discoveries]]. Your own crimes produce '''fines'''. A station
will refuse you service until both are settled: ''"You must get the reward and/or
pay the fines."''

A wanted ship pays its bounty if you or your fleet damaged its hull before it
died, whoever finished it: ''"It doesn't matter if you were the only one who
participated in the destruction of the pirate's ship or someone helped you to
destroy it, you will get a reward in any case."''

=== What a bounty pays ===
A Pirate's bounty is set by its ship and its level, and nothing else: not the
system, not your rank, not who fired the last shot. The claim is held at a
station in the system where it died, or at the nearest station if that system
has none.

* bounty = the ship's base × the level's factor + up to 2,000 at random
* the base is 20,000 for the commonest ships and 110,000 for the rarest
* the factor is 1.85 for Harmless, 1.55 Novice, 1.30 Competent, 1.15 Expert, 1.05 Master and 1.00 Dangerous
* a '''Hyperion''' or a '''Reaper''' adds 150,000

'''The weaker the pilot, the bigger the bounty.''' A Harmless Pirate pays 1.85
times the ship's base and a Dangerous one exactly the base, so the easiest
Pirates in a ship class are also the best paid. '''Rarer ships pay more''': an
Ion is worth less than a fifth of a Goliath.

A '''Criminals Scanner''' ''"scans the ship for the presence on the wanted list"''
and, crucially, '''increases the elimination reward'''. If you intend to hunt, it
pays for itself.

''"Pirates are not wanted in all systems and often they are not marked as enemy
(in red). To find out if there is a reward for a pilot in another system, you need
to scan it with the criminal scanner module."'' Keep a ship targeted within the
scanner's range for five seconds (''"Checking crimes:"''). A scanned Pirate you
destroy pays, four times in five, a second claim at the nearest station in
another system, '''BOUNTY BONUS''', worth half to all of the first. Scanning also
makes ships show their hand: a Pirate turns on you two times in five, and a trader
in a combat ship turns pirate half the time.

'''Conflict Zone''' systems are a running fight between pirates and law
enforcement. ''"You can also help the guards in systems with security level
"conflict zone". Dealing significant damage to a pirate will be richly
rewarded."'' Pirates there go after the law ships, a destroyed pirate is replaced
by another, and three arrivals in ten add a level 5 Hyperion for the law and a
level 5 Reaper for the pirates. Any hull damage you or your fleet deal to a
pirate earns its full bounty, and a pirate Reaper pays 150,000 CR more than other
ships.

Law ships patrol and will scan you for illegal cargo, holding you in place while
they do: ''"Cargo scanning required, please stop and wait."''

=== Silent Mode ===
'''Silent Mode''' is in the external modules menu. ''"If, nevertheless, your ship
is being scanned, then you can turn on the silent mode (in the external module's
menu). This will abort the scan."'' It stops a law enforcement scan for illegal
cargo and a Pirate's scan of your hold, and no scan starts while it is on.

In a fight it ''"acts similarly to chaff launcher, but heats up the ship"'': shots
aimed at you scatter, as they do around chaff. It has costs. Switching it on drops
your shields to zero, they do not recharge while it is on, and the ship heats up
for as long as it runs.

== Pirates ==
Pirates interdict you and will often make an offer first: ''"Drop the cargo – and
I will let you go!"'' Paying is a real option, and a cheap one if your hold is
full of ore you can mine again.

Destroyed pirates leave '''escape pods''', which are cargo you can collect and
sell. The game tracks a daily '''pirates destroyed''' count.

== NPC combat strategy ==
Computer-controlled ships follow a small set of fixed rules. They pick one target,
point their nose at it and fire everything that bears. Knowing those rules tells
you when a fight will end on its own and where their guns cannot reach you.

=== Picking and dropping a target ===
A ship fights back when you hit it while you are targeting it. Pirates also start
fights of their own: a Pirate whose ship is close to yours in value scans your
cargo when you carry more than 3 units, and after the countdown demands ''"Drop the
cargo – and I will let you go!"''. '''Silent Mode''' stops the scan.

An NPC drops you when:
* '''you get far enough away.''' Pirates, traders, law enforcement and mission enemies all give up the chase past the same distance, '''300 light seconds'''. The game's help puts it as ''"At a distance of 250-350 light seconds the pirate ship's sensors will stop working and the pirate will lag behind you."'';
* '''a station is on screen''', for Pirates only. A Pirate targeting you breaks off and idles for five seconds, does not scan you, and does not fight back when you shoot it. The range is measured against your screen size, so it reaches further on a tablet;
* '''you give up the cargo''', for a Pirate: stop attacking and empty your hold, and it says ''"You did the right thing."'' and goes for the boxes;
* '''you surrender to law enforcement.''' With weapons off, both engines off and no illegal cargo it stands down. Come almost to a full stop and it also calls off every ship attacking you, Pirates included, then fines you 4,000 CR: ''"That is better. You have to pay a fine at any station."''

Law enforcement picks a side by who started the fight. If you are fighting a
Pirate or an enemy you have already hit, it helps you. If a Pirate attacked you
first, it goes after the Pirate. If you fired first on anything else, it comes for
you, and every hit you land on it costs 1 [[Combat#Karma|karma]].

=== How they move and shoot ===
* '''Head-on passes.''' An NPC turns toward its target and thrusts at full power. It does not circle, and it does not steer around stations, planets or asteroids. Now and then it breaks away and comes round again.
* '''No weapon choice.''' Every weapon that is in range, pointed at you and powered fires. Fixed guns need you almost dead ahead of the nose; turrets cover their own arc.
* '''No firing at speed.''' No ship fires above speed 15, yours included.
* '''Leading the shot.''' Cannon, Railgun, Pulse Laser and Missile shots aimed cleanly lead you, but only while you are not moving fast to the right or downward on screen. Fly fast in either of those directions and they fire at where you are, not where you will be. Moving left or up, they always lead.
* '''Scatter.''' Your '''Chaff Launcher''' and '''Silent Mode''' spread their shots around you instead of at you.

Law enforcement is always Master; Automatons and Anglers are always Dangerous. An
NPC's weapons themselves are Grade D, or Grade E on Freighters and the
Hyperion.

NPCs also play by looser rules than you:
* '''No power limit.''' Their modules never switch off for lack of power.
* '''No overheating.''' Heat never damages them, and stars do not heat them.
* '''Automatic power, chaff and shield cells.''' You get the same only with the ''Auto power distr.'' and ''Auto attack'' settings.

=== Mines ===
Your [[Combat#Weapons|Mines]] hit every Pirate and every enemy that passes close to
them, whether or not it was fighting you. A mine that hits a Pirate with its
shields down counts as your kill, so its death pays a bounty. Destroyed ships are
replaced by new ones that fly in toward the stations, so the approach to a station
keeps bringing Pirates past a minefield. NPC mines cannot hit you.

== Karma ==
Karma is not a rank you earn, it is a record of how you behave, and the game
gives it names too:

''Despised · Disliked · Average · Liked · Revered''

To see yours, tap your ship and choose '''Missions''' ([[Game Interface#Ship Menu|ship menu]]). That screen is
available whenever your ship is stationary, and shows your karma level and points above your
[[Reputation and ranks|faction reputation]]. Karma is one number for the whole
galaxy, not a standing with each faction.

[[File:Karma on the Missions screen.png|thumb|Karma on the Missions screen]]

It moves both ways. Clearing pirate activity from a system is worth
'''+2'''; destroying law enforcement costs you. It matters because
[[Side quests|side quests]] check it in '''both directions''' — some will not
talk to you until your record is clean, and others will not talk to you unless it
is dirty. A spotless record closes doors as surely as a bad one.
Side quests:
{{spoiler}}
'''42 side quests ship with the game.''' 30 are offered by a named contact in a station's bar, many of them in chains where one must be finished before the next appears; the other 12 start by themselves, out in space. Mods add more in exactly the same format.

You can have '''three side quests''' under way at once. A quest saves at its checkpoints, so a reload puts you back at the last one it reached. If a ship you are protecting is destroyed, the quest fails and is offered again from the start.

'''A white exclamation mark on the galaxy map''' marks a system with a quest waiting. ''"Pay attention to the white exclamation marks on the galaxy map. They mean a side quest is available at one of the stations in the system."'' The mark shows a bar quest you have not taken or finished and whose earlier quests are done. A system shows one mark, and an active mission's mark takes its place.

'''Buy a drink to get a quest.''' The first drink on each visit to a bar offers one quest. Turned it down? Leave, come back and drink again: same quest until you warp. Quests don't show while locked, while your three slots are full, or past 90% drunk.

Some quests are never offered in a bar. They start by themselves the moment you '''arrive in a system''' or '''scan a planet''' inside their area. See [[Side quests#Found in space|Found in space]].

This undermines trust from inside... I will not pull the cat's tail and I will say it straight - I need a mercenary with a good reputation to figure out the mole."''

Modding:
Galaxy Genome loads '''mods''': extra side quests, and extra stars, planets and stations. The game's own [[Side quests|side quests]] are written in exactly the same format, so anything they do, a mod can do. == Mod editor == The fan-made [https://galaxy-genome.github.io/mods/ Galaxy Genome Quest Editor] writes these files for you, in a browser on a phone or computer. Places, ships and conditions are picked from the game's own lists, and it checks a mod against the rules on this page before you copy it to the game. It also has a library of ready-made mods, and downloads the mods you choose as one folder for the game. It is unofficial and not made by SKV Games. To write a mod by hand instead, start with [[Your first quest by hand]] or [[Your first star system by hand]]. == Where mod files go == * '''Side quests''' are files named Quest0.json to Quest199.json. The number only has to be in that range; a quest is identified by the ''ID'' inside it. * '''Stars, planets and stations''' go in one file, StarsStations.json. '''Copy the files straight into the game's own folder on your phone''', with no folder of their own: 
Android/data/com.skvgames.GalaxyGenome/files/Quest150.json
The game only looks for those exact file names in that one folder, so a mod that comes in a folder of its own, like StoryAlt, needs its files moved out of it. Two files with the same number cannot share the folder, so rename one if two mods clash; the number in the name does not matter to the game. On Android 11 and later the phone's own file manager cannot open Android/data. The [https://galaxy-genome.github.io/mods/help/installing Quest Editor's install guide] shows ways around it. Then open '''Modifications''' from the main menu. Each section there shows the '''File Path''' it reads from and whether a mod file '''exists''' in it, which is the quickest way to check the files are in the right place. Switch on '''Side Quests''' or '''Stars and Stations''', and allow the game to access your files when it asks. [[File:Modding mods screen.png|thumb|The Modifications screen with a side quest found and switched on. Each section shows the folder it reads from.]] * '''The game switches every mod off when it updates.''' Turn them back on after each update. * '''[[Combat#Rating battles|Rating battles]] are unavailable''' while mods are active. == A quest file == One JSON object with three parts: settings (who offers the quest and when), BarRumors (optional gossip) and questParts (the steps, in order). A file is skipped without any message when it is not valid JSON, has no settings, has fewer than two steps, or uses an ID another loaded quest already has. Curly quotes pasted into text break the JSON, so check files with a JSON validator. === Example === '''StoryAlt''', the 2021 example mod, is a complete quest to copy from: a dialogue choice with a detour, an ambush, opening a station's menu and a story delivery mission. The copy here is updated to the current format, since the game no longer loads the original. Download it in [https://galaxy-genome.github.io/wiki/files/StoryAlt/Quest150.json English] or [https://galaxy-genome.github.io/wiki/files/StoryAlt/Quest151.json Russian]; both files carry the same ID, so put whichever matches your game's language in the mod folder. [[File:Modding StoryAlt bar offer.png|thumb|StoryAlt's quest on offer in the bar at Thunder Station.]] [[File:Modding StoryAlt choice.png|thumb|The briefing's choice. Each button jumps to a different step of the quest.]] Its settings and two of its steps:

Hopper, Automaton, Walker, Yuri Grom, None, Kaito, Dina, Daily Task, Expedition, Victor, Ruby, Yana Seest === Getting it offered in the bar === The bar offers nothing until the player '''buys a drink'''. The first drink of a visit offers one quest, picked at random from every quest that bar can give right now; accepting or refusing it, or any further drink, brings only jobs and rumours for the rest of that visit. The next offer needs the bar closed and reopened. The random pick stays the same until the player warps, so to test a mod at a station with other quests, warp out and back between tries. Refusing a quest leaves it available. Your quest is only offered when one of the player's three quest slots is free, its Lang matches the game's language, its required quests are finished, and it has not been completed before. Past 90% drunkenness the bar offers nothing until the player has flown long enough to sober up. === Quests that start in space === With isRandomSpaceQuest set, the quest starts by itself when the player '''arrives in a system''' ("RandomSpaceQuestTrigger": "warp") or '''scans a planet''' ("planetScan") within RandomQuestRadius light years of the point RandomQuestX, RandomQuestY on the [https://galaxy-genome.github.io/map/ galaxy map] (Sol is 0, 0). RandomSpaceQuestChance is the chance each time, from 0.0 to 1.0. It only starts when one of the player's three quest slots is free and the quest has not been finished before. === What a mod quest pays === '''A mod's own Reward and KarmaReward are ignored.''' Only the game's own quests pay what they say. A mod quest pays at most '''250 CR''', worked out from the quest itself: * '''150 CR''' if the ships ordered to attack the player cost more than the rest of the ships it spawns, otherwise '''50 CR''' if any ship attacks the player, * plus '''20 CR''' for each step that ends on arriving in a system. A ship counts as attacking only when a shipControl order gives it "SetTarget": "player" and "Attack": true, or it is the target of a pirate-hunt mission. == Bar rumors == BarRumors is a list of gossip lines: {"text": "...", "type": "global"}. Set type to global for a rumor heard in every bar, or local for one heard only in the bar of the quest's own station. == Steps == The quest runs its steps in order. Each step shows its dialogue, spawns its ships, gives its orders, then waits for its completeAction. After the last step the quest is complete and paid. {| class="fandom-table sortable" ! Field !! What it does |- | name || For you; not shown |- | TODO || The line in the player's journal while the step is active |- | questID || A label dialogue options jump to. Steps nobody jumps to can all be 0 |- | isCheckPoint || true: the quest is saved on entering this step, and a reload resumes here. The game keeps no record of a quest before its first checkpoint |- | dialogText || Messages shown when the step starts: Name, showTimeSec, text (under about 320 characters), character, options |- | dialogTextRepeat, repeatTextTimeSec || A reminder shown every so many seconds while the step waits. 999999999 for never |- | completeAction || What finishes the step, from the actions below |- | failureActions || Actions that fail the quest, separated by ; |- | shipSpawn, shipControl || Ships to spawn and orders to give (below) |- | task_on_station || A mission offered at a station during the step (below) |} * '''Choices.''' options puts buttons under a message: "2=Head straight for Wolf 359;10=Check Ross 720 first;". A button jumps to the step whose questID is that number; -1, or a number no step has, carries on in order. * '''Actions are written without BUTTON_.''' The game adds that prefix itself, so BUTTON_ACTION_SHIP_DESTROYED_Hunter never matches. * '''A failure needs every listed action.''' "A;B" fails the quest only once both have happened during the step. A failed quest can be taken again from the start. * '''Don't make a fight a checkpoint.''' To put a station in an existing system, list that system in Stars with its exact X, Y, Z, security and type as the [[Galaxy Genome Map|map]] shows them. A matching entry overwrites all of them: a guess moves the system, a missing security makes it Anarchy, and a missing type makes it an M-RedDwarf. === What PlanetID counts === PlanetID counts every body listed for the system, from 1. For an existing system the bodies the game already lists come first, then this file's planets in order. Asteroid belts count, and a station can orbit one; it then has no visible body to circle. Companion stars count too, but a station cannot orbit one and is skipped. === Security levels === {| class="fandom-table sortable" ! security !! Pirates among ships !!
